blocks.text: My Lord, as the jury know we're moving on to another baby this morning, a baby by the name of [Baby N]. If I could invite everybody, please, to go to their jury bundle number 1, behind divider 1, please. If I can invite everyone please to turn to page 6.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: (No audio feed from court)
Witness statement of [MOTHER OF BABY N] (read)
-- in her statement she says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am the mum of [Baby N] who was born at 1.42 pm on 2 June 2016 at the Countess of Chester Hospital. I am in a relationship with [Father of Baby N], who is [Baby N]'s dad.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was a normal pregnancy up to about 24 weeks when the hospital identified he wasn't growing properly, so we were going for weekly scans to check his growth.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I think it was at our 32-week scan when they booked me in for a caesarean section because they needed him to come out as soon as possible in case the placenta failed.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We were booked in for 2 June 2016. Because he [being [Baby N]] had haemophilia, he needed to have a few extra people in theatre in case of a bleed during his delivery. He was born at 33 weeks and didn't have any bleeds during the caesarean. He was small, only 3 pounds, 11 ounces, and he was quite jaundiced and he went straight into the neonatal unit. He went ahead of us and I didn't get to visit him until about 10 pm on the night of 2 June.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "One of the midwives took me down and when we got there, [Baby N] was in the first room to the left of the intensive care room, called nursery 2. Nobody was with him when we got there and I wasn't introduced to anyone at that time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As far as we were concerned, he was only in the unit purely because of his prematurity and it wasn't until day 13, 15 June, that we were made aware of any problems. There weren't any major issues prior to that, just keeping his temperature stable and initiating feeding. His temperature had dropped and they were trying to raise it. He had a feeding tube in and they were trying to establish a feeding routine. It all seemed fairly normal and we visited [Baby N] daily.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "They were working with Alder Hey on a plan in case [Baby N] had a bleed while he was so young. He had been brain scanned and there were no bleeds.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "During those first 13 days I remember a nurse called Catherine and there were other nurses too that I remember: one called Lucy
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: and a foreign lady whose name began with M, possibly Minna. I remember Lucy and Catherine looked after [Baby N] quite a bit and another nurse who was from Liverpool called Bernie.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On the 12th day, 14 June, we were told by a consultant he was able to go home the next day. [Baby N] was in nursery 4 by that point. I was due to go and collect him on 15 June.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Around 8 am on that day I had a phone call from [Baby N]'s dad, [Father of Baby N], to say there'd been an issue at the hospital and that [Baby N] had had a bleed and was unwell but it was nothing to worry about. I rang the hospital to clarify whether I needed to take a car seat in with me and was told by a lady called Grace to go into the neonatal unit as soon as possible.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I got there around 9 am and [Father of Baby N] got dropped off from work and we met there. I saw lots of people when I got there. [Baby N] was in intensive care and had never been there before. I remember Lucy was there and the lady I think was called Minna. It was a very emotional time when I went in that morning and the consultants were just trying to keep him stable.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We were told they had tried to intubate him between 4 am and 8 am and that he'd had a bleed when they were trying. They carried on trying whilst we were there. An anaesthetist tried and couldn't do it. Dr Saladi was also unsuccessful so it was a long-drawn-out process during the day, during which time he had another two collapses.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When I say collapses, I mean where his heart went really low and they gave him CPR. We were told to go out and get some fresh air in between his two collapses. Whilst we were out, he had his second collapse.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we got to the evening and he had his second collapse, I think it was actually Alder Hey staff who were there and who got the tube in. Lucy was our main point of contact through the day because she was tending to [Baby N] in between the consultants being with him.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We'd had [Baby N] baptised during the day and that was recommended to us by Lucy. It was a spur of the moment thing that we agreed to do as we thought anything might help. We saw the priest in the morning and came back in the evening, when the Alder Hey staff were there, and baptised [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We had been in touch with the haematology nurses from Alder Hey beforehand and so the transfer team brought with them the factor VIII medicine that [Baby N] needed as Chester did not have any in stock, even though they knew he was a haemophiliac before he was born. Chester only had my factor VIII from my caesarean, as
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I am also a haemophiliac, and they had to use that to give to [Baby N]. The staff that came from Alder Hey was a massive team and included a nurse called Cathy who was also a haematology nurse. There were also the doctors from intensive care and an ear, nose and throat doctor. Lucy stayed on past the end of her shift until [Baby N] left for Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] went initially to intensive care when he arrived at Alder Hey where they stabilised him. He was already intubated and they told us he was okay. He was only in intensive care for a couple of days."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, that completes the relevant parts of [Mother of Baby N]'s statement.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of [FATHER OF BABY N] (read)
If I could move next, please, to the statement of [Father of Baby N] dated 14 November 2019. [Father of Baby N] says the following:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My partner is [Mother of Baby N] and we have a son together, [Baby N], who I call [Baby N]. [Baby N] was born at the Countess of Chester Hospital on 2 June 2016. [Mother of Baby N] is a haemophilia carrier, so in pregnancy she needed to have extra factor [as he puts it]. We knew when [Baby N] was born that he would have haemophilia and potentially need factor after his birth.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When [Mother of Baby N] was pregnant with [Baby N] she went for a scan appointment. I was self-employed at the time so I couldn't go to all the scans with her. I'm not sure of the date but after one particular appointment [Mother of Baby N] told me they were concerned that [Baby N] appeared to have stopped growing. As a result, [Mother of Baby N] had to have steroids to bring [Baby N]'s lungs on.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Because of the concerns about [Baby N]'s growth they decided that [Mother of Baby N] should have a caesarean several weeks early. The caesarean went ahead as planned on 2 June 2016 and I was in the room when [Baby N] was born at around 2 pm. When [Baby N] was born he only weighed 3 pounds, 11 ounces. We found out later that day that the Countess of Chester did not have any factor in the hospital. We were surprised they had not arranged to have some available knowing that [Mother of Baby N] was booked in for a caesarean that day and that [Baby N] would be born with haemophilia. Fortunately, there were no issues with this on the day. It was a little scary when he was first born as he needed a little oxygen, but he was fine and there were no other issues.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After his birth, [Baby N] was taken to the neonatal unit. [Baby N] stayed in the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital for 13 or 14 days. Until the last day the only issues he had were his bilirubin levels. This is to do with the liver. A couple of times when I went to see him he was on light therapy for this.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Since [Baby N] was born, [Mother of Baby N] and I went to see [Baby N] in the neonatal unit every day. [Mother of Baby N] stayed in hospital for about a week after the caesarean. Once [Mother of Baby N] came home we went in to see [Baby N] every day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As time went on, [Baby N] moved from the first room to the second room next door and then the third room next to the second. The day before [Baby N] took ill, he'd been in the third room. On the day [Baby N] was due to come home from the Countess of Chester Hospital, I am not sure of the day or date, but [Baby N] was 13 or 14 days old, I was at work. I then received a phone call from [Baby N]'s nurse, Lucy. Lucy said that [Baby N] had been a bit unwell in the night and she said he's okay now.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I told Lucy that [Mother of Baby N] would be in in a bit to see him as usual and that was that. She didn't give me any other information. I did not get the impression that he was still unwell or that we needed to be concerned. About 10 minutes later, [Mother of Baby N] rang me. We needed to go to the hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was about 9 am when we arrived at the neonatal unit. [Baby N] was in the ITU room and Lucy was in the room with him. He was in the far right corner. Lucy was by his bed; I think she was either checking the monitor or doing his cares, changing him. She was stood on the opposite side of the bed to the monitor but in and around the area of the cot. There were no other staff in the room at that time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "There was no urgency. When we arrived Lucy just said, 'Hi, he's been a bit unwell in the night'. When I say [Baby N], I felt shocked looking at him as his skin was bluish in colour. This bluish colour was all over his body. I think he was only wearing a nappy. He had dry blood around his lips and around the outside of his mouth on his skin. His lips were not fully covered in blood but loads of blood was spattered over them like he'd coughed. The blood was dry, so it was a dark, reddy-brown colour. I know [Baby N] was not wearing an oxygen mask or anything over his mouth as I clearly remember seeing the blood.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "He may have been on oxygen via tubes in his nostrils, but I can't remember. I remember feeling confused and thinking, what's wrong with him, as his stats on the monitor were normal and he
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: seemed stable. His stats remained stable while we were in the room, they did not dip.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I think Dr Saladi may have been in and out of the room but no one told us what happened or why.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After [Baby N] had been stable for a couple of hours, [Mother of Baby N] and I decided to nip out for some food as neither of us had eaten that day, it was about 11 am or 12 noon or even a bit later. We were probably gone 20 to 25 minutes in total when we got back to the main doors into the neonatal unit, the parents whose baby was also in ITU were sat outside the unit. We were buzzed into the neonatal unit and we walked in. I noticed that all the blinds were down in the ITU room. They'd previously been up.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Someone came from the nurses' desk to speak to us. They said [Baby N] was really unwell and that we could see a priest. I sat outside the door to the ITU for a bit, I was scared. [Mother of Baby N] went into the ITU.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "A priest then came and we went around the side and into the back room, the family room where you can stay overnight. We then went back round to ITU. [Mother of Baby N] went in and I waited outside.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] then seemed to stabilise for a bit and I went into the ITU room with [Mother of Baby N]. I couldn't say for how long. [Mother of Baby N] had been feeling unwell all day so as [Baby N] was stable, they said we could get a doctor to see [Mother of Baby N]. We went through the doors to the maternity unit and [Mother of Baby N] saw a doctor. It might have been Dr Saladi, I'm not sure. I think I waited outside the room while they examined [Mother of Baby N]. Someone then came into the maternity unit and said something similar to, 'You'd better come, he's bad again, he's really ill this time'.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I'm not sure how long we'd been in the maternity unit when she came to get us. We ran up the corridor to the ITU. When we arrived they were doing resuscitation on [Baby N]. There were a lot of people in there seeing to [Baby N]. I'm not sure who as I didn't go in at that point, but [Mother of Baby N] went in.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After about 5 minutes I went in. I had my back to the cot because I couldn't watch them doing resuscitation on [Baby N]. There were two anaesthetists in there. One of them was explaining how they had tried to get a breathing tube in and they couldn't get it in. There was a woman in a green cardigan; I think she was the doctor. There were also people from Alder Hey Children's Hospital in there, although they might have arrived slightly after.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "There was a woman from Alder Hey and a fellow from Alder Hey. The fellow eventually got the breathing tube in [Baby N]. I don't know his name but I've seen him in Alder Hey since and when I saw him, I couldn't thank him enough for that.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "After the breathing tube was fitted, [Baby N] stabilised a bit. When I say stabilised he wasn't having CPR, he seemed okay, he'd calmed down. I'm not sure if he was sedated. We then went to speak to a haemophilia nurse, Cathy, in another room. Cathy had come over in a taxi from Alder Hey with some factor. After we'd spoken to Cathy we went back to the ITU.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we were back in the ITU, the NWTS team, which is the transport team, came in. They had a blue capsule which was to transport [Baby N] into Alder Hey. The transfer of [Baby N] to the NWTS, the transport team, seemed to last forever. It actually took a couple of hours to put him in their capsule. He had tubes coming off him. By the time they were ready to transfer it was quite late in the day, about 11 pm. Just before we left the Countess of Chester Hospital, we were sat outside ITU on chairs. There were a lot of people in the ITU room seeing to [Baby N] so we were staying out of their way. Lucy then came up to us and told us she had stayed on late, past the end of her shift, she said to [Mother of Baby N], 'I hope he's all right', and gave [Mother of Baby N] a hug. She might have given [Mother of Baby N] a kiss, I'm not sure. [Baby N] was then taken to Alder Hey by the NWTS team in an ambulance and we followed behind the ambulance.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "When we arrived at Alder Hey we sat in a side room for a couple of hours while they were setting him up. By the time they'd done this, it was the early hours of the morning. They let us stay in a side room on the ward just down the corridor from [Baby N]. [Baby N] stayed at Alder Hey Hospital for about 2 weeks. He was downgraded from ITU to HDU and then came home.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Once at home, [Baby N] was having little twitches. We didn't think anything of it at first, but then started having little spasms. On one occasion he was struggling to breathe. We were not taking any chances so we phoned an ambulance. We were taken to the main accident and emergency unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Someone from Alder Hey, a paediatrician, came to the Countess to see [Baby N]. [Baby N] was then transferred back to Alder Hey again by the NWTS. We did not receive a diagnosis as to what was wrong with him. [Baby N] was stable whilst he was in Alder Hey. He just did nothing but improve again. He was there for about 1 or 2 weeks and they said he could come home."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, that concludes the statement of [Father of Baby N].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, we're going to move on to the first of two sequences of events for [Baby N]. Just so that the jury understands the way (inaudible: no microphone) one sequence and a neonatal unit review for count 17, then we'll do the other two counts because they happened on the same day on the same shift in a single consequence (inaudible: no microphone) evidence (inaudible: no microphone) sequence (inaudible: no microphone) between those we will have the evidence of (inaudible: no microphone) sequence (inaudible: no microphone).
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MRS CLAIRE HOCKNELL (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Welcome back, Mrs Hocknell. Would you, for the sake the recording, please, confirm your identity?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Claire Hocknell.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Are you responsible for the preparation for a sequence of events presentation concerning the events of 3 June, in fact the 2nd into 3 June 2016, which corresponds to count 17 in the indictment?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. If we start, then, please, at tile 1. Does this record that on 2 June, prior to the birth of [Baby N], there are some obstetric medical notes concerning [Mother of Baby N], who is the mother of [Baby N]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: At tile 2, is that some material that was downloaded from Lucy Letby's Facebook account time at 11.48 showing that she then connected with [Dr A] on Facebook Messenger?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Count 3 at 11.49, a minute later, did [Dr A] send Lucy Letby a message?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Hi Lucy. Are you working Sunday or next week? I need a favour. More like an opinion on something and wondered if you'd mind? No problem if you can't! [Dr A]."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Did Lucy Letby respond 4 minutes later?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Hi [Dr A]. I'm on nights at the moment, on days next Wednesday, Friday and Sat if that helps."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we go to tile 6 next, please, and could you tell us what [Dr A] next sent to Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Sorry if I disturbed you. I'm in Wednesday and Friday on normal days. Thanks."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then back to count 5 -- tile 5, sorry.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "No, not at all. Okay see you next week."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Those messages are produced, not obviously, in the wrong order, so to speak, in the sequence. Is that because that's how they appear in the download from the phone?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's a direct representation of how they appear in the download, but as per the conversation, it appears that they may because slide 5 and slide 6 are both at 11.56 and indeed they may appear out of sequence.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Does that lead us to the point that you don't --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't manipulate it.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: You don't manipulate the data at all, you simply produce what the --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, factually as it appears.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you very much. That will be left as it is because that is the way the data is produced, but as a matter of fact, those two messages appear to be the wrong way round?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: All right. Did Lucy Letby then respond, at tile 7, 10 minutes later at 12.06?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Hope I can help."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Is tile 8 a record of [Baby N]'s birth at 13.42?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: That same day, he was 34 plus 4 weeks' gestation, born by elective C-section, weighing 1.67 kilograms. Apgar scores recorded as 9 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes respectively?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. At tile 9, was he admitted to the NNU at 14.00 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Underneath that tile, have you recorded his observations?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: The jury will be given that material in hard copy in due course. At tile 10, is there a nursing note written by Caroline Oakley?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: I would like to deal with most of this material as we go through because there are very few live witnesses for this particular incident, so if we can go behind that, please, and if you would talk us through what appears in the nursing notes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Admitted 14.00 due to prematurity and intrauterine growth restriction. [Query] clotting disorder. Cord bloods taken as requested. Baby weighs 1.67kg. Colour: pink. Respiratory rate: 64 breaths per minute, apex 144 and temperature 36.7."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Do we then at tile 11 have a record made of [Baby N]'s heart, respiratory and -- heart rate, respiratory rate and temperature --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: -- together with the cot temperature? At tile 12 were some swabs taken to screen for MRSA?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then at tile 13 were some bloods collected, which were ultimately reported on by the lab?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. At tile 14, is there a record of some donor breast milk being attributed to [Baby N] at 14.45 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then at tile 15, at 14.50, are there some clinical notes of Dr Ukoh?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. For the same reasons as before, I'd like to deal with what these actually say, please. Could you take us through what Dr Ukoh recorded?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Male infant admitted on to neonatal intensive care unit today from labour ward theatre with..."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: I think that's an element of notes I wasn't able to decipher.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: It may be "clotting problems" in this context.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Birth weight 1.670 kilos. (1) Prematurity: 34 plus 4. (2) Intrauterine growth restriction. Again, 1.67 kilos. (3) Maternal carrier of haemophilia, baseline factor VIII, 23%. Low level factor VIII. Maternal risk factors for sepsis. Prom fever. Apgars 9 at 1 minute, 9 at 5 minutes. Had antenatal dextrose x2 doses on 17 May and 18 May 2016. Last scan was 31 May 2016, 34 plus 1. Established foetal weight 1.542. Positive EFD. Elective caesarean section for intrauterine growth restriction. 34.4 baby boy. Cried immediately. Required no active resuscitation. Mother: [Mother of Baby N], 28 years.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Plan: admit to the neonatal intensive care unit. Cord blood sent for APTT/factor VIII. Not for IM vitamin K for now until haemophilia status known. [Query] oral vitamin K, but prem baby. If continues grunting/respiratory distress, partial septic screen plus IV antibiotics."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Is that then followed by some observations, which included Dr Ukoh's own examination where he recorded:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Small baby plus facial acrocyanosis, intermittently grunting ++. Grunting, res mild (overspeaking) plus" --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "[Respiratory] mild. [Subcostal] and [intercostal] recession."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Transmitted upper airway noises."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And then some other observations, including a capillary refill time of less than 2 seconds, centrally soft abdomen...
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Non-tender."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "... non-tender. Tender nil mass. Diagram in notes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Both testes descended."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: When you said -- I haven't looked at the note, does it say -- you said "established weight".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Does it just say "est" --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Est", estimated.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: I was going to say.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: You can't establish a weight when it's --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Estimated, yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Thank you. Anyway, going on to 16, please. At 3 pm, were [Baby N]'s vital signs recorded on the chart that we've seen many times?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: At 17, there are some more bloods reported, received, which were ultimately reported upon?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: At 18, a further record of some expressed breast milk in the neonatal feeding chart?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: At 19, 15.10, on an apnoea/bradycardia/fit chart, was it there recorded:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Crying, dropped sats, 60% oxygen via Neopuff"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I was one of the daytime paediatric registrars covering the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital on 2 February 2016. I attended the delivery of [Baby N]. blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, there are a number of tiles which could be referred to during the course of these statements.

blocks.text: "A review of the maternal notes shows that [Baby N]'s antenatal anomaly scans had been normal and there were no risk factors for sepsis (for example premature rupture of membranes, maternal sepsis or fever or maternal group B streptococcus).
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Mum had received two doses of antenatal steroids to help with maturation of baby's lungs in case of an anticipated preterm baby. There had been concerns about intrauterine growth restriction on growth scans. Mum was known to be a carrier of
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: haemophilia A and there was pre-emptive advice from the consultant haematologist about checking the baby's cord blood for APTT (a test to check clotting status) and also factor VIII (the clotting factor that is low in haemophilia A).
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "According to the notes, paediatric senior house officer Dr Vikash Jankee and myself met with parents on the labour ward (inaudible: coughing) delivery around 9.50 am. We explained to the parents that we would be present at the delivery due to prematurity, would provide any respiratory support needed, and discussed the possibility of some babies needing resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We discussed that baby would be admitted to the neonatal unit for observation, respiratory support and feeding support as needed, and explained that due to his prematurity it may take time to establish on breast or bottle feeds and there is a possibility of needing a nasogastric tube for feeding initially. Consent was taken for the use of donor-expressed breast milk.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We explained about [Baby N] being low birth weight and preterm and would need an incubator for temperature control. We offered the parents a tour of the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] was born on 2 June 2016 at 13.42 at 34 weeks and 4 days' gestation by elective caesarean section. His birth weight was low at 1.67 kilograms. He cried immediately and had good Apgar scores of 9 out of 10 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "He was brought to the neonatal unit and initial observations on admission were satisfactory. I then handed over to my colleague, a locum paediatric registrar, who assessed the baby at 14.50. According to my colleague's notes, at about 1 hour of age [Baby N] was found to have some intermittent grunting, increased work of breathing, cool peripheries, and some transmitted upper airway sounds. This is not unusual in babies born by caesarean section due to excess fluid on the lungs. The usual practice is to observe for 4 hours to see if these symptoms settle down before considering a sepsis screen.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The baby's cord blood was sent for clotting investigations as per haematology advice and intramuscular vitamin K was withheld in case of increased bleeding or bruising with injection until the results were back, as advised by Dr Mark Caswell, consultant paediatric haematologist at Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I next saw [Baby N] on the ward round the next morning, that is 3 June 2016, at 11 am."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: This note is behind tile 231 if anyone wants to make a note:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] had been eventually screened for sepsis the previous day due to persistence of the intermittent grunting beyond 4 hours of age as per local neonatal guidelines and was now on antibiotics with a differential diagnosis of either TTN or possible sepsis.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "He had also been kept nil by mouth on intravenous fluids in view of his respiratory distress to prevent choking or aspiration. On the ward round he was breathing without any support in room air and had oxygen saturations of 100%. I noted that he had had an episode overnight at around 1.10 am when his oxygen saturations had dropped to 40% along with colour change and duskiness (and was reviewed by my colleague Dr Loughnane soon after) but had settled thereafter and did not need
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: supplemental oxygen for very long. His blood gas in the morning was satisfactory. On examination he had mild sternal recession (indrawing of the sternum or breastbone during breathing, a common sign of increased work of breathing in newborn babies, especially those born prematurely) and a respiratory rate of 60
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: per minute with no nasal flaring or grunting, which are other signs of respiratory distress in babies.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The rest of his examination was unremarkable and he was pink, well perfused, with normal heart sounds and femoral pulses, normal abdominal exam, normal anterior fontanelle, and no bruising. Overall, he seemed to be doing well from a respiratory point of view. I was therefore happy for him to have some enteral feeds, (they are milk feeds through a bottle or nasogastric tube if not interested in the bottle) at 50% of his
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: required daily rate and to slowly increase as tolerated.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "He was to continue with antibiotics at least until the blood culture results came back at 36 hours and I requested a blood test for repeat CRP (C-reactive protein), an infection marker.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby N] had also developed jaundice in the first 24 hours of life and was receiving phototherapy treatment for this. It was planned to continue this and repeat bilirubin levels for jaundice in the evening.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "His clotting tests from the day before were abnormal, suggestive of a diagnosis of haemophilia A, and I therefore made a plan to discuss again with the haematology team at Alder Hey Children's Hospital for further advice (this was subsequently done by my locum colleague). His cranial ultrasound scan (to look for obvious bleeds in the brain) from the previous day was
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: normal. I did not have any further input in [Baby N]'s care."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tiles 203 to 206 are four separate records made of the giving of the drugs that we have seen earlier prescribed to [Baby N] at 8 o'clock when attempts were being made to intubate him?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: At tiles 207, 208 and 209, do we have three sets of data filled in on the charts that we see so often on the hour, every hour, this time at midday?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: At tile 210, timed at 12.34, some more door swipe data recording the entrance of Lucy Letby into the neonatal entrance?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Followed at tiles 211 to 213 by the three sets of data recorded on the manuscript charts at 13.00 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: So do we then come to [Dr A]'s response to Lucy Letby's update sent to him about [Baby N]'s condition and her apology saying, "Sorry if I was off during intubation, Bernie winds me up", et cetera?

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Could you tell us what he said to her, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "No, you were perfectly fine with me. I couldn't tell who you were annoyed with, but the look on your face when taking wrappers off the top of the intubation trolley was priceless. blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Did [Nurse E] then respond to a message that Lucy Letby had sent her earlier?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Did she say:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "No worries. How is it?"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Is that followed by, at 13.16, door swipe data showing the entrance of Lucy Letby into the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: At 13.17, did Lucy Letby respond to [Nurse E]'s question, "No worries, how is it"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, she said:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Mad but getting straight. [Nurse B] went for her scan, then Yvonne and Jean gone to Liz dad funeral. Minna not too pleased with it, not ideal staffing. Baby G okay, bled a bit more but had factor VIII now and seems okay."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: And another message:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Are you okay?"
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Did [Nurse E] respond:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Didn't know about Liz's dad, that's sad. Glad Baby G looking better. Not good bleeding with his haemophilia. So is [Nurse B] having all her AN appointments in work time? I know you're entitled, but she's only in 3 days a week."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Did she follow that up with:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I've got a banging headache and feel like I've been living in a desert"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Do we then have several entries relating to the prescription and administration of cefotaxime and sodium chloride between 13.21 and 13.30?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Followed by, at tile 225, Dr Henton's clinical notes relating to some blood tests, apparently, by the look of it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Then followed thereafter by some more text messaging, which perhaps you could start with at tile 226 and I'll do the other side of the conversation, if I may.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby replied to [Nurse E]:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "No, bit [worried] about him this morning. Looks that way! With shift work should be able to go on days men really [as read]."
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Oh no".
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: Did [Nurse E] respond at tile 228, 13.45 hours:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Just remembered my yogurt is in the fridge, so have it if get chance or it will end up in bin"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 13.50, Lucy Letby then replies to [Dr A]:
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: "Oops. I kept clearing the trolley and she was making more mess and then she [spilt] half the sux putting it into a different syringe when didn't need to. Wanted to get it done ASAP. blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: That is shown on the screen as being to [Nurse E], but that in fact is an error, isn't it, on the screen?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: So we'll have that corrected, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's clearly a response to the earlier one from [Dr A].
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 2.30, I think she then responded:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Ha ha, cheers."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And [Nurse E] sent two messages in quick succession saying:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Don't say I never give you anything!"
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Presumably referring back to the yogurt. Then:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Baby G's parents been in."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HOCKNELL

blocks.text: My Lord, we are just leading up to the immediate prequel to the next event. If we're going to have a break, this might be the better place.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think that'll do for this afternoon for the jury. We'll continue at 10.30 tomorrow morning.

blocks.text: Thank you very much.

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
I've read all the paperwork. There are, in respect of one of the witnesses, two applications.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. [Dr D], an application for screens, and also an application for reporting -- a reporting condition. The first may be less controversial than the second. Can I concentrate on the second? It's a very detailed statement, [Dr D] giving background to her personal circumstances.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Just let me ask Mr Myers.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Do you have any observations in relation to either of the applications?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We don't, my Lord, no.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. Well, I'll deal with the application for a screen first of all because that seems to me to be quite straightforward.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm satisfied on the material that has been presented by and on behalf of this particular witness that it is appropriate that she be granted the special measures direction that she has requested, namely that she be screened when giving her evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving on to the second part of her application, we're conscious there's a careful balance to be struck. We have given it careful consideration and we respectfully submit that (inaudible: no microphone) striking that balance (inaudible: no microphone) given the particular combination of personal circumstances and very, dare I say, understandable concerns about press reporting, that this is a case that falls just in favour of allowing, please, this application.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, without ventilating the matters in public, it's a constellation of issues. It is just not a simple issue, there's quite a long background in relation to --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't want to ventilate them in court.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And very responsibly, Mr Myers has not sought to make any submissions in relation to it. And although I appreciate it is a significant order that is being sought in this case, which is effectively providing anonymity for the purposes of general reporting of the identity of this witness, I am satisfied that it is appropriate for the reasons that have been given earlier in relation to other witnesses that such an order should be made. Of course the witness will be identified in court.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So her identity will be known to those in court and the jury will be unaware of the fact that there is going to be any reporting restriction as such of her identity. But I'm satisfied it is appropriate the order should be made.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. That leaves the second application or second witness.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I should say that obviously the position of the person at the material time can be reported.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it's just the name, essentially --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- that cannot be reported.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. It will be in the same terms.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The media have behaved very responsibly in relation to the orders that have been made.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We're frequently asked for reminders and we always give them, so everybody is aware.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Moving on to the second application, it's simply screens.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Again, I have read the material in relation to that and this particular witness.

blocks.text: Mr Myers has nothing that --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Nothing to add, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS
